1205.title: The family of Benedict
1205.hook: Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists: many branches of one Rule
1205.howItsDone: Benedictine, Cistercian and Trappist monasteries each follow the Rule of Saint Benedict, with their own constitutions and customs, and some welcome visitors to their prayer and retreat houses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a little rule: Benedict's own name for his Rule, written for beginners. Your line was always beginning.

Two monasteries. In the first, the church is tall and richly decorated, and the monks spend long hours in sung prayer, the liturgy unfolding in full ceremony. In the second, the walls are plain, the windows clear, the monks out in the fields in rough habits, and the church so bare it almost echoes. Ask the monks in either place what they live by, and they'll hand you the same small book. Today: the family of Benedict.
screen: `A TALL CHURCH AND LONG CHANT.` → `PLAIN WALLS AND MUDDY FIELDS.` → `THE SAME SMALL BOOK.`

segments.voice: Benedict wrote for monasteries, not for an order. Each house was its own family, under its own abbot. So how did one rule produce such different houses? Part of the answer is in the Rule itself: it's built to bend. In chapter eighteen, after laying out which psalms are sung when, Benedict says anyone who finds a better arrangement may use it, as long as the whole psalter is still prayed each week. In chapter fifty-five, clothing should suit the place and the climate. Again and again the abbot is told to weigh things, adjusting for the weak and the strong. A rule that expects to be adapted gets adapted. Three branches people still name. Cluny, in Burgundy in France, became known for its liturgy: long, splendid prayer in the choir, and other houses linked themselves to it. The Cistercians took their name from Cîteaux, another French monastery, where monks set out to keep the Rule more strictly and simply: plain churches, hand labor, Benedict's life stripped back to its lines. Saint Bernard of Clairvaux was a Cistercian. And the Trappists, named for the abbey of La Trappe, came out of a reform within the Cistercians seeking a stricter observance still; officially they're the Cistercians of the Strict Observance. Cluniacs and Cistercians argued, sometimes sharply, about what keeping the Rule really required. Yet each was reading the same chapters: listen, stay, bear with each other. One rule, many houses.
screen: `MONASTERIES, NOT AN ORDER.` · `A RULE BUILT TO BEND.` · `CLUNY, CÎTEAUX, LA TRAPPE.` · then, large: `ONE RULE, MANY HOUSES.`

segments.voice: Somewhere right now, in a house of one of these branches, monks and nuns are at work, or in choir, or asleep before an early office: the old one in the infirmary, the novice still learning the chants, the one in the kitchen. If you pray, hold them before God for these two minutes; if you don't, simply keep them company in your attention, without needing to know their names.
The family of Benedict. The monasteries and orders that live by his Rule, Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists and others, each reading it in its own way. Today's word.
Your line: one rule, many houses. The branches argued, and still read the same book. That's today, done.

1206.title: Oblates
1206.hook: laypeople who follow the spirit of the Rule in ordinary life
1206.howItsDone: Benedictine oblates attach themselves to a particular monastery, make an oblation after a period of preparation, and try to live the spirit of the Rule at home through daily prayer, spiritual reading and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the family of Benedict: Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists, one Rule read in many ways. Your line was one rule, many houses.

A nurse finishing a night shift. A retired mechanic. A mother of three who keeps a worn copy of the Rule in the glove compartment. None of them lives in a monastery or wears a habit. But each belongs, in a real way, to one particular abbey, and tries to live by Benedict's Rule in a house with a mortgage and a washing machine. The family of Benedict has a branch that doesn't live behind any wall at all. Today's word: oblate.
screen: `A NURSE, A MECHANIC, A MOTHER.` → `NO HABIT, NO CLOISTER.` → `BENEDICT'S RULE AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Oblate means one who is offered. The word goes back to the Rule itself. In chapter fifty-nine, Benedict describes parents who offer a son to the monastery: they wrap the boy's hand, with their written promise, in the cloth of the altar, and so give him to God. That custom ended long ago. But the word stayed, and came to name something new: men and women outside the cloister, single or married, who offer their lives to God in the spirit of the Rule while staying exactly where they are. Today an oblate attaches to one particular monastery, usually after a time of getting to know it. In a short ceremony they make an oblation: a promise to live by the spirit of the Rule as their life allows. It's a promise, not the vows of a monk. They don't move in, or give up their homes or marriages. What they take home is the shape of the life: some of the psalms and prayers the monks pray, morning or evening; a daily time of slow reading with Scripture; work done carefully, as if the tools were altar vessels; guests received as Christ. And a link to their monastery, which prays for them and which they visit when they can. Stability, in a different way: tied to one house, carrying its rhythm into a kitchen, a classroom, a hospital ward. The Rule was written for people behind walls. Oblates show that it fits through a front door.

1207.title: A Benedictine day at home
1207.hook: a bell, a psalm, work, reading, a meal, silence
1207.howItsDone: Some Benedictine oblates and other laypeople shape their day around short times of the Liturgy of the Hours, a period of lectio divina, focused work and shared meals, adapted to family and job.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oblates: laypeople tied to one monastery, carrying the Rule into ordinary life. Your line was the rule at home.

Six things. A bell. A psalm. Work. Reading. A meal. Silence. That's the whole list, and it's almost too plain to write down. But lay those six out across a day and something happens to the day. It stops being one long smear of tasks and screens and becomes a set of rooms, each with a door. Today, the last day with Benedict, a simple question: what does it look like put together, in a house that isn't a monastery?
screen: `A BELL, A PSALM, WORK.` → `READING, A MEAL, SILENCE.` → `A DAY WITH DOORS.`

segments.voice: Start with the bell. In the Rule, the bell isn't a nag. It's a signal that the next thing has come, and at the signal for prayer, Benedict says, monks put down whatever is in their hands and go: nothing before the work of God. At home the bell might be an alarm, the kettle, a church bell down the street. Then the psalm. The monks pray at set hours, from the night office to the last prayer before sleep; at home it may be one psalm, morning or evening. Then work. Idleness, Benedict writes, is the enemy of the soul, so there are hours for work with the hands, and the tools are handled like the vessels of the altar. Then reading: hours set aside for slow, attentive reading of Scripture. Then a meal, eaten with others while someone reads aloud, with food and drink that's enough and not too much. Then silence, especially after the last prayer at night. The thread through every piece is balance. Benedict keeps asking for measure. He wants the abbot to arrange everything so that the strong have something to strive for and the weak have nothing to run from. Prayer doesn't swallow work. Work doesn't swallow reading. In chapter sixty-four, Benedict calls this good judgment discretion, the mother of virtues. So the Benedictine day isn't impressive. It's proportioned. Tomorrow the path leaves the monastery and walks out on the road with Francis of Assisi.

segments.voice: Look at the rest of your day and choose one hour you could shape: a psalm, then work with no phone in reach, a short stretch of reading, a meal eaten slowly. 1208.title: Kissing the leper
1208.hook: Francis writes that what was bitter became sweet
1208.howItsDone: Franciscans tell the story of the leper as the start of Francis's conversion, and Franciscan friars and sisters still serve the sick and the poor in hospitals, shelters and missions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Benedictine day at home: bell, psalm, work, reading, meal and silence, kept in balance. Your line was balance.

Francis of Assisi left a short text now called his Testament, looking back at how it all began. A reader might expect a vision, a voice from heaven, a dramatic call. Instead he starts with his stomach. When he was living in sin, he says, the very sight of lepers was too bitter for him to bear. That's where the story of the Franciscans opens: not with a great deed, but with a man who couldn't stand to look at certain people. Benedict's cloister is behind us now; this is the road, and the friars. Today: kissing the leper.
screen: `FRANCIS LOOKS BACK.` → `NOT A VISION. A REVULSION.` → `OUT OF THE CLOISTER, ONTO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's what Francis says happened. The Lord himself led him among the lepers, and he showed them mercy. And when he left them, what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, of soul and of body. Then, he says, he waited a little while, and left the world. A few lines, and in his own telling, the hinge of his whole life. Notice what he doesn't say. There's no kiss. The kiss comes from the stories his early biographers told. In their telling, Francis is riding near Assisi when he meets a leper on the road. Everything in him wants to turn the horse around. Instead he gets down, gives the man money, and kisses his hand, and the leper kisses him back. In some versions he then goes to the place where lepers lived and serves them there. Francis's own spare account, and the vivid scene the biographers drew: both land on the same turn. Look at who does what in the Testament. Francis doesn't say he conquered his disgust. He says the Lord led him. The change in his feelings came after the mercy, not before it. He didn't wait to feel sweetness before he went; the bitterness changed on the way out. That suggests the feeling of revulsion isn't a verdict. It can be the doorway. In the gospels Jesus touches a leper before he heals him.

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that makes you pull back, not something dangerous, just a call you've avoided or a person you steer around, and notice where the feeling sits in your body without arguing with it. Then picture yourself doing it anyway, gently, the way Francis got down from his horse, and see whether the picture changes the feeling at all. If you pray, ask to be led, the way Francis says he was.

1209.title: The gospel as the rule (1208)
1209.hook: Francis hears Matthew 10 at Mass and decides to live it literally
1209.howItsDone: Franciscan friars take the gospel as their rule of life, and the Rule of Saint Francis opens by naming the observance of the holy gospel as the life of the brothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kissing the leper: Francis showed mercy, and what was bitter turned to sweetness. Your line was bitter became sweet.

A small chapel outside Assisi. A Mass. The priest reads the gospel, the same way gospels get read every day, and the room may well have heard this one before. One man in the chapel hasn't heard it like this. It's the passage where Jesus sends his disciples out with almost nothing. When Mass ends, the man asks the priest to explain it. And when the priest is done, he says, in his biographer's telling: this is what I want. This is what I've been looking for. Today: the gospel as the rule.
screen: `A MASS NEAR ASSISI.` → `A FAMILIAR GOSPEL.` → `THIS IS WHAT I WANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the passage, from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims. Jesus tells the twelve: "Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your purses: Nor scrip for your journey, nor two coats, nor shoes, nor a staff; for the workman is worthy of his meat." A scrip is a traveler's bag. So: no money, no bag, no spare coat, no shoes, no walking stick. Go, and trust that you'll be fed. Words like these can be heard as a picture of an attitude: hold things loosely. Francis took them as instructions. His early biographer says he took off his shoes on the spot, put down his staff, kept a single tunic, and swapped his leather belt for a piece of rope. Then he went from place to place, preaching peace and repentance. Later, in his Testament, Francis said no one showed him what to do; the Most High himself revealed that he should live according to the form of the holy gospel. Benedict wrote a rule and pointed beyond it to Scripture. Francis tried to skip the middle step. When his brothers later needed a written rule, its opening line said, in effect: the rule and life of the brothers is this, to observe the holy gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. The gospel wasn't the inspiration for the rule. It was the rule. The biographer doesn't say which gospel writer's version was read; the sending passages in Matthew, Mark and Luke are close cousins. What he tells is the response: Francis heard it and did it, literally.

1210.title: Little brothers
1210.hook: the friars minor, the lesser brothers
1210.howItsDone: Franciscan friars call one another brother, and their superiors are called ministers and guardians rather than abbots or priors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gospel as the rule: Francis heard Jesus send the twelve out with nothing, and did it. Your line was take nothing.

Names for leaders tend to climb. Manager, senior manager, director, vice president, chief. Every title is a step up, and everyone can see who's where. Francis's small band of followers needed a name. Some readers hear in his choice an echo of the Italian towns of his day, where, they say, the powerful were called the major people and everyone else the minor people. Either way, Francis picked the low side, and he put it right in the name. Today's word: friar.
screen: `TITLES THAT CLIMB.` → `THE MAJOR AND THE MINOR.` → `FRANCIS PICKS THE LOW SIDE.`

segments.voice: Friar simply means brother. Francis's companions were the fratres minores: the lesser brothers, the little brothers. That's still the official name, the Order of Friars Minor. His early biographer tells how it happened. When the words of the rule were being written and they came to the phrase, let them be lesser, Francis said: I want this brotherhood to be called the Order of Lesser Brothers. In the earliest rule the brothers kept, the idea runs all the way through. Nobody is to be called prior, which means the one who comes first. All are lesser brothers, and they wash one another's feet. Even those put in charge are called ministers, which means servants. It echoes a gospel scene. The disciples argue about which of them is the greatest, and Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you not so: but he that is the greater among you, let him become as the younger; and he that is the leader, as he that serveth." Friars are also a different shape of religious life from the monks who promise stability. They don't live behind a monastery wall for good. They go out, into towns and along roads, among ordinary people, preaching, working, begging when they must. Monks stay; friars move. The Church recognizes both as ways of giving a life to God. But a friar's whole identity starts from below: lesser, by choice, and brother, to everyone.

1211.title: Lady Poverty
1211.hook: Francis marries poverty like a knight marries a lady
1211.howItsDone: Franciscan friars and Poor Clares make a vow of poverty, owning nothing personally, and Franciscan laypeople try to live simply and share with the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the friar: one of the lesser brothers, who chose the low side on purpose. Your line was lesser brothers.

Before he was a saint, Francis wanted to be a knight. His early biographers tell of a cloth merchant's son with fine clothes, generous with his friends, who rode off to war dreaming of glory, and came home changed. He never quite lost the knight's way of talking. In the old tales of chivalry, a knight pledged his life to a lady and fought in her colors. Francis found a lady too, and she was not a person at all. Today's word: poverty.
screen: `A MERCHANT'S SON WHO WANTED GLORY.` → `KNIGHTS PLEDGE THEMSELVES TO A LADY.` → `FRANCIS FINDS HIS LADY.`

segments.voice: Francis's biographers say he spoke of poverty as his lady, even as his bride, the one he'd chosen above every other; Saint Bonaventure writes that he called her by those names. An early allegory goes further, telling of Francis and his brothers climbing a mountain to find Lady Poverty and take her as their companion. It's a love story, not a budget. Francis's poverty wasn't stinginess or a grim rule. It was courtship. He went without so his hands would be free for Christ, and for the people Christ loved. Behind it are two lines of Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims. Jesus tells a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me." And Paul writes of Christ: "being rich he became poor, for your sakes." Francis wanted to follow the one who became poor. It cost him. His father, a cloth merchant, brought him before the bishop of Assisi to demand his money back. Francis gave it back, and then, the story says, took off his clothes, laid them at his father's feet, and said that from now on he would call God his father. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Poor for love, not poor for its own sake. These days have set two ways of giving a life to God side by side: Benedict's houses under one Rule, and Francis on the road.

segments.voice: Choose one small thing to go without, the second coffee, the new purchase, the background noise, not as a punishment or to prove anything, but the way Francis did: as making room. Then ask who that room is for, a person who could use the cost, or the time. If you pray, offer the empty space to God.
